a: Brothers
t: Brothers, and later brothers and sisters
p: The preacher calls his hearers "brothers" until 19:1, where he says "brothers and sisters".
b: Greek adelphoi, 'brothers'. As in the site's 1 Clement and the Epistle of Barnabas, the Plain English Translation keeps the word as the Greek has it, since in Greek the masculine plural can include women. In 19:1 and 20:2 the preacher says adelphoi kai adelphai, 'brothers and sisters', and the translation changes there so that the reader sees the change. Lightfoot took those two places as proof that the work is a sermon spoken to a mixed congregation, not a letter (see the note at 19:1).

a: as we think of God
p: The sermon opens by telling the church to think of Jesus Christ as of God and as the coming Judge.
b: The Greek is short: houtōs dei hēmas phronein peri Iēsou Christou, hōs peri theou, 'so we must think about Jesus Christ, as about God'. It does not argue the point; it takes for granted that the hearers already speak of Christ in this way, and draws from it how seriously they must take their salvation (1:2). Lake names this 'high Christology' as one of the sermon's three aims, with 'a pure life' and the resurrection of the flesh. The sermon later says that Christ 'was spirit at first and became flesh' (9:5), and gives God's sayings and the Lord's sayings the same weight (13:4).

a: the Judge of the living and the dead
t: Judge of the living and the dead
p: A phrase from the apostles' preaching, which later went into the creeds.
b: Lake's margin points to Peter's speech to Cornelius: "God has marked him out to judge the living and the dead" (Acts 10:42). The same pair stands in 2 Timothy 4:1 and 1 Peter 4:5. 'The living and the dead' means everyone, those still alive when he comes and those already dead. The preacher returns to the judgment again and again (9:1; 16:3; 17:4-7; 18:2).

a: how much Jesus Christ endured to suffer for our sake
p: Four things to know: where they were called from, by whom, to what, and what Christ suffered.
b: The sentence is the outline of the opening section. Where they were called from: the idols and the 'death' of their old life (1:6; 3:1). By whom: Christ, who called them 'when we were perishing' (1:4; 2:7). To what place: the kingdom and the rest to come (5:5). What it cost: his suffering. Lightfoot's summary of the chapter puts the stress on this last point: to think lightly of Christ is to think lightly of the salvation he suffered to win.

a: in return
p: A business word runs through the sermon: what return can we make to God?
b: Greek antimisthia, 'payment in return' (1:3, 5; 9:7; 15:2), with the related misthos, 'pay, reward' (1:5; 3:3; 9:5; 11:5; 19:1; 20:4). The preacher is not saying that God sells salvation. He asks what a grateful person can give back for a gift that cannot be repaid, and his answers are confessing Christ by deeds (3:3), sincere repentance (9:7-8), and speaking and listening with faith and love (15:2). The same word is used of the reward God pays (11:6), so the two halves of the sermon, what we owe and what we will receive, use one vocabulary.

a: he granted us the light
p: Light, sight and darkness frame the opening: the hearers were in a mist and now see.
b: The preacher uses the picture of light and darkness for conversion: 'we were wrapped in darkness ... But we have received our sight again' (1:6). The letter to the Hebrews speaks of believers as 'those who once received the light' (Hebrews 6:4), and Acts 26:18 of opening the eyes of the Gentiles 'so they turn back from darkness to light'.

a: We bowed down to stones and wood, gold, silver and bronze
p: The preacher and his hearers were Gentiles who had worshiped images before they became Christians.
b: This is the clearest fact the sermon gives about its first hearers. They had bowed down to images 'that people had made' and say so of themselves ('we'). The list of materials is the one the Bible uses against idols: 'Their idols are silver and gold, / something human hands have made' (Psalm 115:4); compare Daniel 5:4, 23 and Revelation 9:20. Lightfoot made the point a reason why the writer cannot be Clement of Rome: this preacher 'delights to identify himself and his hearers with Gentile Christianity', while 1 Clement writes as an heir of Israel. Paul reminds the Thessalonians how they 'turned away from idols to God' (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

a: received our sight again
p: The verb is the one the Gospels use when Jesus heals the blind.
b: Greek aneblepsamen, 'we looked up again, recovered sight'. In Mark 10:52 the same verb tells of the blind man Bartimaeus: 'At once he could see again'. The preacher uses it again at 9:2 ('In what did you receive your sight, if not while you were in this flesh?'), so that healing from blindness becomes his picture of what happened to his hearers' minds, which had been 'maimed' (Greek pēroi, a word for the crippled or blind).

a: out of nothing
p: Being saved is described as a second creation, from what does not exist.
b: Greek ek mē ontos, 'out of what is not'. The words echo the Jewish teaching that God made the world from nothing, as the mother says in 2 Maccabees 7:28 ("God made them, not from things that were"), and Paul's God 'who makes the dead alive and calls the things that are not as though they were' (Romans 4:17). Here the preacher applies the picture to the hearers' conversion: when they 'did not exist' as God's people, he called them into being.

a: Be glad, barren woman, you who bear no children!
t: Isaiah 54:1 in Greek, as Paul quotes it
p: The preacher quotes Isaiah 54:1 in the Greek Bible's words, exactly as Galatians 4:27 does.
b: The Greek here is word for word the Greek of Galatians 4:27, so the Plain English Translation uses the site's Galatians wording: "Be glad, barren woman, you who bear no children! Break out and cry aloud, you who have no labor pains! For the children of the desolate woman are many, more than those of the woman who has a husband." The site's Isaiah 54:1 is made from the Hebrew and reads differently: "Sing for joy, you barren one who has borne no child!" Paul uses the verse for 'the Jerusalem above', who 'is our mother' (Galatians 4:26). The preacher goes his own way and explains it line by line (2:1-3), the first of several places where he reads a text phrase by phrase in the manner of a sermon.

a: our church was barren
t: The barren woman is the church
p: Before the Gentiles believed, the church had no children; now it has more than Israel.
b: The preacher reads the barren woman as 'our church' and the woman 'who has a husband' as the people who 'seemed to have God' (2:3), that is, the Jewish people. Lightfoot read the passage that way: the Gentile church has more children than the Jewish people 'who seem to have God'. It is an early example of reading a promise to Zion as a promise to the church gathered from the nations. On the site, the chapter pages of Isaiah 54 give the passage's meaning for its first hearers, the exiles in Babylon.

a: not lose heart like women in labor
p: A puzzling turn: women in labor cry out, and the preacher says not to lose heart as they do.
b: Greek mē hōs hai ōdinousai enkakōmen, 'let us not grow weary like women in labor'. The verse he explains tells the barren woman to cry out because she does not have labor pains. He takes 'cry aloud' as prayer, and the pains of labor as the weariness that makes people give up praying. The verb is the one Luke uses for not giving up in prayer: 'they needed to pray at all times and not grow weary' (Luke 18:1). Lake translates 'and not grow weary as women that give birth'.

a: those who seemed to have God
p: A sharp contrast between the young Gentile church and the Jewish people of the preacher's time.
b: The 'woman who has a husband' stands for 'those who seemed to have God'. Paul could say of his own people that "they have zeal for God" (Romans 10:2) and that "God does not take back his gifts and his call" (Romans 11:29); the preacher says only that they 'seemed' to have God, and counts the church's growth in numbers as the proof. Lightfoot remarked that the preacher's language about Church and Synagogue 'would probably have been more guarded' if he had written after Marcion (who taught that the God of Israel was not the Father of Jesus). Christians today read such early statements in the light of Romans 9-11; see the topic page on the church.

a: another Scripture also says
p: The preacher quotes a Gospel saying with the formula used for the Old Testament.
b: He has just quoted Isaiah, and goes on: 'another Scripture also says', and quotes a saying of Jesus found in Matthew 9:13 and Mark 2:17 in the same words ("I did not come to call righteous people. I came to call sinners"; Luke 5:32 adds 'to repentance'). George Reid, writing on the canon in the Catholic Encyclopedia, called the sermon the place 'in which we find, for the first time after 2 Peter 3:16, the word Scripture applied to a New Testament book.' Lightfoot compared the Epistle of Barnabas, which introduces 'many called, but few chosen' as Scripture (Epistle of Barnabas 4:14), and Polycarp to the Philippians 12:1. Whether the preacher means a written Gospel or a collection of sayings is not said; see the sections on the sayings of Jesus in the opening pages.
orig: ἑτέρα δὲ γραφὴ λέγει (hetera de graphē legei)

a: Christ also willed to save what was perishing
p: Lake's margin points to Luke 19:10.
b: Jesus says to Zacchaeus: 'The Son of Man came to look for what was lost and to save it' (Luke 19:10). The Greek words differ (the Gospel's 'what was lost' is a perfect participle, the preacher's 'what was perishing' a present one), so the Plain English Translation follows the preacher's own words. He draws the contrast in 2:6: anyone can hold up what is standing; the wonder is to hold up what is falling.

a: dead gods
p: The living do not sacrifice to the dead: a stock Jewish and Christian argument against idols.
b: The preacher puts 'we who are living' against 'dead gods', as the Bible sets the living God against idols that cannot see or hear (Psalm 115:4-8; Jeremiah 10:10). Paul praises the Thessalonians for having turned 'to serve a God who lives and is true' (1 Thessalonians 1:9). The word 'sacrifice' is concrete: in a Greek or Roman city, sacrifice to the gods was part of ordinary public life, and refusing it marked Christians off from their neighbors.

a: What is knowing him, then
p: True knowledge of the Father is shown by not denying the Son.
b: Greek tis hē gnōsis hē pros auton, 'what is the knowledge that is toward him?' The word gnōsis, 'knowledge', is not yet the 'knowledge' of the later Gnostic groups; the preacher uses it in a plain sense. Lake's footnote on 'him' says: 'The Greek is as ambiguous as the English, but this "him" no doubt refers to the "father of truth."' Knowing the Father is proved by not denying the one through whom we know him, which leads straight to the saying about confessing Christ (3:2). Compare 1 John 2:23: no one who denies the Son has the Father.

a: I will confess him in front of my Father
p: A saying close to Matthew 10:32 and Luke 12:8, but in other words.
b: Matthew 10:32 reads: "So everyone who openly declares for me in front of people, I too will declare for that person in front of my Father in heaven." Luke 12:8 has 'in front of God's angels'. The preacher's form is shorter and uses 'me' instead of the Gospels' 'in me'. The site's Gospels say 'openly declares for' for homologeō; here the Plain English Translation says 'confess', because the preacher builds three verses on the one verb (3:2-4; 4:3: 'let us confess him by what we do').

a: with our whole heart and our whole mind
p: The words of the great commandment, applied to confessing Christ.
b: Lake puts the words in quotation marks. They come from the command to love God 'with all your heart, with all your being, with all your mind and with all your strength' (Mark 12:30; Deuteronomy 6:5). The preacher sets them against honoring God 'with our lips' only, the point of the Isaiah verse he quotes next.

a: This people gives me honor with their lips
p: The short form of the Gospels (Matthew 15:8; Mark 7:6), but with the verb of 1 Clement 15:2.
b: The preacher's Greek agrees word for word with 1 Clement 15:2 (apestin, 'is away'), except that the two put 'this people' in a different order, and differs from Matthew 15:8 and Mark 7:6, which have apechei, 'keeps away'. So the Plain English Translation uses the site's 1 Clement 15:2 wording: "This people gives me honor with their lips, but their heart is far away from me." The site's Matthew 15:8 reads "but their heart keeps far away from me." The two writings that were copied together in Codex Alexandrinus and the Constantinople manuscript also share 'the prophetic word' of 11:2-4 (1 Clement 23:3-4). The site's Isaiah 29:13 is made from the Hebrew and is longer: 'this people draws near with its mouth / and honors me with its lips / but has moved its heart far from me'. The preacher says 'he also says in Isaiah', naming the prophet as the place of a saying of the Lord.

a: Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will be saved
p: Close to Matthew 7:21, but with 'will be saved' and 'does what is right'.
b: Matthew 7:21 reads: "Not all who call me 'Lord, Lord' will get into the kingdom of heaven. The one who will get in is the one who does what my Father in heaven wants." The preacher has 'will be saved' for 'will get into the kingdom', and 'the one who does righteousness' for 'does what my Father wants'. Lake's margin gives Matthew 7:21. Whether the preacher quotes Matthew from memory, another written Gospel, or sayings passed on by word of mouth is the question behind all his quotations; see the opening pages.

a: self-controlled
p: The virtue the preacher later says his whole sermon has been about (15:1).
b: Greek enkrateis, from enkrateia, 'self-control' (as the site's Galatians 5:23 renders it). In 15:1 he calls his whole sermon 'the advice I have given about self-control'. He means mastery of the desires of the flesh, keeping 'the flesh pure' (8:4, 6; 14:3). Lightfoot noted the sermon's 'Encratite tendencies', a leaning toward the strict self-denial of the later Encratites ('the self-controlled'), who rejected marriage and wine; the preacher himself never forbids marriage (see 12:5).

a: we must not fear people more than God
p: The line prepares for the sayings about wolves and Gehenna in 5:2-4.
b: The thought is the apostles' answer: "Obeying God has to come before obeying people" (Acts 5:29) and Jesus' word in Matthew 10:28, which the preacher gives in his own form at 5:4. The order of the sermon suggests why he says it here: confessing Christ by deeds may bring danger, and the danger is not to be feared more than God.

a: Even if you are gathered with me in my embrace
t: A saying of the Lord in no Gospel
p: Lake: its source 'is unknown'. Its ending is close to Matthew 7:23 and Luke 13:27.
b: No Gospel has the opening words. Lake's note: 'The source of this and the quotation in v. 2-4 is unknown: it is often supposed to have been the Gospel of the Egyptians, but there is no clear evidence of this.' His margin marks both places 'Ev. Aegypt.' The picture of being held 'in my embrace' (Greek kolpos, as the site's John 13:23, 'reclining in Jesus' embrace') makes the warning harder: even the closest disciple who does not keep the commandments will be thrown out. The ending recalls Luke 13:27 ("I don't know where you are from. Leave me, all you workers of wrong!") and Matthew 7:23 ("Leave me, you who practice lawlessness!") but is not the Greek of either: the preacher's 'I do not know you' (ouk oida hymas) is in neither verse as the site gives them. See the topic page on sayings of Jesus outside the Gospels.

a: our stay as resident aliens in this world
p: The Christian's life on earth is a foreigner's stay in a city that is not home.
b: Greek paroikia, the stay of a paroikos, a foreigner living in a city without citizen rights. The word stands in the greetings of 1 Clement 1:0 and Polycarp to the Philippians 1:0, where the church 'lives as a resident alien' in its city, and goes back to 1 Peter: 'live in fear during your time as resident aliens' (1 Peter 1:17). The preacher draws a hard lesson from it: let us leave our stay here behind and not be afraid to 'leave this world'. In 5:5 he uses a second word for the same idea, epidēmia, a visitor's stay. See the topic page Strangers and Exiles: Christians as Resident Aliens.
orig: τὴν παροικίαν τοῦ κόσμου τούτου (tēn paroikian tou kosmou toutou)

a: Let us not be afraid to leave this world
t: Not afraid to leave this world
p: Does the preacher mean death for the faith, or giving up the world's way of life?
b: Lightfoot thought the false teachers the preacher opposes 'permitted their disciples to deny their faith in times of persecution', and the sayings that follow, about lambs among wolves and those who kill (5:2-4), point to the danger of death. The verse can also be read more broadly, of the readiness to give up this world's goods that 5:6 describes ('treat the things of this world as belonging to someone else'). The sermon does not name any persecution, so both readings rest on its words alone.

a: Peter answered him
t: A dialogue between Jesus and Peter in no Gospel
p: 5:2-4 joins Gospel sayings into a conversation that no Gospel has.
b: The saying 'like lambs surrounded by wolves' is close to Luke 10:3 ("I am sending you like lambs into the middle of a pack of wolves") and Matthew 10:16. Peter's question and Jesus' answer are found in no Gospel, but the answer ends in words close to Matthew 10:28 and Luke 12:4-5. Lake's note: the source of 4:5 and 5:2-4 'is unknown: it is often supposed to have been the Gospel of the Egyptians, but there is no clear evidence of this.' Peter speaks for the disciples here as he often does in the Gospels (Matthew 18:21; Matthew 19:27).

a: The lambs should not fear the wolves once they are dead
p: A command: the wolves can do no more once they have killed, so the believer's true danger lies elsewhere.
b: The saying turns the picture of 5:2 into an argument. The wolves stand for those who kill; once a lamb is dead, the wolf has done all it can. The Greek is a command in the third person (mē phobeisthōsan, 'let them not fear'), and the next words turn it to the disciples: 'And you, do not fear'. Only God has authority after death, so only God is to be feared. The same logic stands in Luke 12:4-5: 'do not fear the people who kill the body. After that there is nothing more they can do.'

a: the fire of Gehenna
p: The valley outside Jerusalem that gave its name to the place of final punishment.
b: Greek geenna pyros, 'Gehenna of fire', the phrase the site's Matthew 5:22 and 18:9 render 'the fire of Gehenna'. Gehenna is the Valley of Hinnom south of Jerusalem, where children were once burned in sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31), and which became in Jewish and Christian teaching the name for the place of punishment after the judgment. Many English Bibles say 'hell'. The site keeps the name, as in the Gospels.

a: our stay in this world, in this flesh
p: A second word for life on earth: a visitor's stay.
b: Greek epidēmia, a stay away from home, a visit. With the 'resident aliens' of 5:1 it makes the point twice: this world is not home, and the stay is 'small and brief'. Against it the preacher sets 'rest' (anapausis) in the coming kingdom, a word he uses again at 6:7. Jesus promises rest to the weary (Matthew 11:28), and Hebrews speaks of the Sabbath rest that 'is still waiting for God's people' (Hebrews 4:9).

a: as belonging to someone else
p: Treat this world's goods like property in a foreign city: not yours to keep.
b: Greek allotria, 'belonging to another, foreign'. The word fits the picture of 5:1: a resident alien lives among things that belong to the citizens. The preacher draws the moral in 5:7: wanting to get them is what makes people fall off 'the right road'. Compare 1 Timothy 6:17-19.

a: No household slave can be a slave to two masters.
p: The saying in exactly the Greek of Luke 16:13; Matthew 6:24 lacks 'household'.
b: The preacher's Greek is that of Luke 16:13, so the Plain English Translation uses the site's Luke wording. Matthew 6:24 has 'No one' instead of 'No household slave'. He then applies the saying in his own words, with 'we' (6:1b).

a: wealth
p: Greek mamōnas, from an Aramaic word for wealth or property.
b: Older English Bibles keep the word as 'mammon'. The site's Gospels render it 'wealth' (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13), and the sermon follows them. It is not the name of a god; Jesus speaks of money as if it were a rival master.

a: loses his soul
t: Winning the world, losing the soul
p: Close to Matthew 16:26, Mark 8:36 and Luke 9:25 (Lake's margin).
b: The site's Matthew 16:26 reads: "What good will it do a person to win the whole world and pay for it with his life?" The preacher's Greek is shorter and differs at the start ('what is the gain'). The Greek word psychē can mean 'life' or 'soul'; the site's Gospels say 'life', and the Plain English Translation of the sermon says 'soul' because the preacher uses the word for the soul throughout (12:3-4; 16:2; 17:1).

a: This age and the age to come are two enemies
p: Jewish teaching spoke of 'this age' and 'the age to come'; the preacher makes them enemies.
b: The two ages are a Jewish way of speaking that Jesus and Paul share ('not in this age and not in the age that is coming', Matthew 12:32; 'the rulers of this age', 1 Corinthians 2:6). The preacher goes further: the two are 'enemies', so that no one can be friends with both (6:5). James says the same of the world and God: 'being the world's friend means being God's enemy' (James 4:4). Greek aiōn means both 'age' and 'world'; Lake translates 'the world that is, and the world to come'.
orig: οὗτος ὁ αἰὼν καὶ ὁ μέλλων (houtos ho aiōn kai ho mellōn)

a: says goodbye to them
p: The verb for taking leave, used of giving up the world.
b: Greek apotassetai, 'takes leave of, says farewell to'. It is the verb of Luke 14:33: 'none of you can be a disciple of mine if he does not say goodbye to all his possessions'. The preacher uses it three times (6:4, 5; 16:2), and the Plain English Translation keeps 'say goodbye' each time so the reader can follow it.

a: eternal punishment
p: The phrase of Matthew 25:46.
b: Greek aiōnios kolasis, the words of Matthew 25:46: 'these people will go off to eternal punishment, and the righteous will go to eternal life'. The preacher sets it against 'rest' as Matthew sets it against 'eternal life'. Whether such punishment is endless or ends in destruction is a question the churches answer differently; the site's card at Matthew 10:28 sets out the views.

a: Even if Noah and Job and Daniel stand up
p: A free summary of Ezekiel 14:14-20, with 'in the captivity' added.
b: Ezekiel names three righteous men who could save only themselves if God judged a land: 'and Noah, Daniel and Job were in it, as I live, the Lord GOD declares, they would not save a son or a daughter' (Ezekiel 14:20). The preacher gives the names in another order, says 'their children', and adds 'in the captivity', which Ezekiel does not say there; Ezekiel was himself among the exiles in Babylon (Ezekiel 1:1). He uses the verse to argue from the greater to the lesser: if such men cannot rescue even their children, we cannot count on anyone's righteousness but our own (6:9). Lake's margin: Ezekiel 14:14, 18, 20.

a: keep our baptism pure and unstained
p: The preacher speaks of baptism as something to be guarded after it is received.
b: This is the first of three places where the sermon tells the hearers to keep what they received at baptism: 'keep our baptism pure and unstained' (6:9), 'those who have not kept the seal' (7:6), 'keep the flesh pure and the seal spotless' (8:6). He does not say what happens to someone who sins seriously after baptism, but he calls for repentance 'while we have time' (8:2; 16:1). The churches' views of what baptism does are set out in the site's cards on baptism (for example at Romans 6 and 1 Peter 3); the sermon assumes all its hearers are baptized. Lake's margin compares Matthew 22:11-13, the guest thrown out of the wedding feast because he had no wedding clothes.

a: our advocate
p: Greek paraklētos, the word for Christ in 1 John 2:1.
b: A paraklētos is someone called to stand beside a person on trial. 1 John 2:1 says 'we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ', and John's Gospel uses the word for the Holy Spirit (John 14:16). The preacher asks who will plead for us if we have no holy and righteous works: the advocate must have something to point to.

a: let us compete
p: The athletic language of the games runs through this chapter and returns in 20:2.
b: Greek agōnizōmetha, 'let us compete', and agōn, 'contest', the words for an athletic or musical contest at the great games. The preacher uses them nine times in chapter 7 and again in 20:2 ('competing in the trial of the living God'). Paul used the same picture for the Corinthians: 'Everyone who competes controls himself in everything. They do it to receive a crown that fades. We do it for one that never fades' (1 Corinthians 9:25).

a: many sail in for contests
p: Lightfoot thought this pointed to the Isthmian games near Corinth.
b: Greek katapleousin, 'they sail in, land'. Lightfoot argued that a preacher who says simply that the crowds 'land' for the games, without naming the port, is speaking near the place where they land, and that the Isthmian games, held at Corinth's isthmus between two seas, fit best. Lake reports this as Lightfoot's view of where the sermon came from (see the opening pages). Lightfoot also recalled that Paul's own 'perishable and imperishable crown' was written to Corinthians (1 Corinthians 9:25). The digital Greek text has a slip here (katapleousa); Lake's printed page reads katapleousin.

a: not all are crowned
p: At the games, only the winner received a crown of leaves.
b: Greek stephanoutai, 'is crowned'. The prize at the great Greek games was a wreath, not money, and only one competitor won it. The preacher bends the picture: in the contest that does not perish, 'all of us may be crowned' (7:2), and those who cannot win should 'at least come close to the crown' (7:3). The New Testament promises 'the crown of life' (James 1:12; Revelation 2:10) and 'the wreath of glory that never withers' (1 Peter 5:4).

a: is whipped, taken away and thrown out of the stadium
p: At the Greek games, officials with rods beat competitors who broke the rules.
b: Lightfoot's note on 'whipped' names the officials who did it, the 'rod-bearers' or 'whip-bearers' of the games, and cites Herodotus and Thucydides for blows given 'in the contest' to those who broke the rules. The preacher's question follows in 7:5: if cheating in a contest for a perishable prize brings such shame, what will cheating in the contest of incorruption bring?

a: cheats in the contest of incorruption
p: A play on words: the one who 'corrupts' the contest of 'incorruption'.
b: Greek ho ton tēs aphtharsias agōna phtheiras, 'the one who has corrupted the contest of incorruption'. The same root runs through 7:1-5: 'perishable' contests (phthartos), 'cheating' (phtheirōn, 7:4), 'incorruption' (aphtharsia). English cannot keep all of it; 'cheats' gives the sense. The preacher returns to the play in 14:3-5: whoever 'corrupts' the flesh will not share in 'incorruption'.

a: those who have not kept the seal
p: The seal means baptism: Lake's English translates 'the seal of baptism'.
b: Greek sphragis, 'seal', the mark pressed into wax or clay to show ownership. The preacher uses it for baptism again in 8:6 ('keep the flesh pure and the seal spotless'), with 'keep our baptism pure' in 6:9 as the plain form of the same thought. Lake makes the meaning explicit in his English ('the seal of baptism'); the Plain English Translation keeps the preacher's word. The New Testament uses the verb for the Spirit given to believers (Ephesians 1:13; 2 Corinthians 1:22).

a: a spectacle to all flesh
p: The last verse of Isaiah, in the Septuagint's form: 'a spectacle', where the Hebrew has 'a horror'.
b: The site's Isaiah 66:24 is made from the Hebrew and ends: 'For their worm will not die, / and their fire will not be put out, / and they will be a horror to all flesh.' The preacher's Greek has eis horasin, 'for a sight, a spectacle', so the Plain English Translation keeps the site's first two lines and says 'a spectacle' in the last. Jesus uses the same verse of Gehenna (Mark 9:48: "where their worm never dies and the fire is never put out"). The preacher quotes it again at 17:5, there in the mouth of the Lord's judgment.

a: we are clay in the craftsman's hand
p: The prophets' picture of the potter, turned into a warning about time running out.
b: Jeremiah watched a potter remake a ruined vessel and heard the LORD say: "Look, as clay is in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand, house of Israel" (Jeremiah 18:6). Paul uses the potter for God's freedom (Romans 9:20-21). The preacher adds a detail of the workshop: a pot can be reshaped while the clay is soft, but once it has been fired in the kiln it cannot be changed. The kiln stands for death (8:3).

a: we can no longer confess our sins or repent there
p: The preacher says plainly that repentance is possible only in this life.
b: This is the sermon's reason for urgency (8:1-2; 9:7; 16:1). It agrees with Hebrews 9:27 ('it is in store for human beings to die once, and after this, judgment') and the parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:26). The churches differ on whether sins can be cleansed after death for those who die in God's grace: the site's cards at 2 Maccabees 12:45 and Matthew 12:32 give the views. The preacher's point is narrower: no one can begin to repent after death.

a: the Lord says in the gospel
t: "In the gospel": a saying part found, part not
p: The first half is in no Gospel; the second is Luke 16:10 word for word.
b: The second half of the saying has the Greek of Luke 16:10, so the Plain English Translation uses the site's wording: "someone who is faithful in the smallest things is faithful in big things as well." The first half ('If you did not keep what is small, who will give you what is great?') is close in thought to Luke 16:11-12 but is not in any Gospel. Lake's margin prints 'Luke 10, 10-12', a slip for 16:10-12. The phrase 'in the gospel' may mean a written book or the message of Jesus; the sermon never names an evangelist.

a: keep the flesh pure and the seal spotless
t: The preacher's reading of the saying
p: He applies 'faithful in small things' to keeping the body pure.
b: The 'small' thing of 8:5 is life in the flesh, and the 'great' thing is eternal life. The preacher turns the saying from money (as in Luke 16) to the body: whoever does not keep the flesh pure here will not be trusted with eternal life. The 'seal' is baptism (see 7:6). The change of person, 'keep' and then 'that we may receive', is in the Greek; Lightfoot defended it as a common turn of speech. C and the Syriac smooth it away with 'that you may receive' (see the variant).

a: this flesh is not judged and does not rise
t: Against denying the resurrection of the flesh
p: Some in the preacher's church said the body would not rise or be judged.
b: Lightfoot thought this the doctrinal point the preacher 'especially dwells' on: the 'resurrection of this flesh' (8-9; 14; 16). Those who denied it, in his reading, drew the conclusion that what the body does does not matter (compare 10:5). Paul met the same denial at Corinth ('how is it that some among you say no resurrection of the dead exists?', 1 Corinthians 15:12), and 2 Timothy 2:18 names men who said 'that the resurrection has already taken place'. The preacher answers from experience: you were saved and healed in the flesh (9:2), so you will be judged and rewarded in it (9:4-5).

a: as a temple of God
p: Paul's words to the Corinthians: the body is a temple.
b: Paul writes: "your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you" (1 Corinthians 6:19), and of the whole church, "you are God's temple" (1 Corinthians 3:16). The preacher uses the picture for the flesh, and draws a different conclusion: a temple must be guarded from what defiles it.

a: was spirit at first and became flesh
p: A short statement that Christ existed as spirit before he became flesh.
b: Greek ōn men to prōton pneuma, egeneto sarx, 'being at first spirit, he became flesh'. The words recall John 1:14 ('the Word became flesh'), but say 'spirit' where John says 'Word'; one Greek manuscript (C) indeed reads 'Word' here (see the variant on this verse). Lightfoot called the passage 'the doctrine of the pre-existence of the Son, as the Logos, ... presented in a somewhat unusual form', and set it beside the Shepherd of Hermas, which calls the Son 'that Spirit', and Tertullian's 'the Spirit of the Creator, which is Christ'. Whether 'spirit' here names Christ's divine nature or confuses him with the Holy Spirit is the question; the Plain English Translation writes 'spirit' in lowercase so as not to decide it. The preacher's own argument is about the flesh: if Christ came in flesh, our flesh matters.
orig: ὢν μὲν τὸ πρῶτον πνεῦμα, ἐγένετο σάρξ (ōn men to prōton pneuma, egeneto sarx)

a: God, our healer
p: God's name at the spring of Marah: 'the LORD, your healer'.
b: At Marah God told Israel: "For I am the LORD, your healer" (Exodus 15:26). The preacher speaks of repentance as being healed while there is still time. The sermon has already quoted the saying that goes with Jesus' words about the doctor in Mark 2:17 ("People who are strong do not need a doctor. Sick people do"); see the note at 2:4.

a: so that he may welcome us as sons
p: The verse returns to 1:4: God, 'like a father', addressed us as sons.
b: Greek hina hēmas prosdexētai hōs huious, 'that he may receive us as sons'. The thought is adoption (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:5-7). 'Sons' is the Greek word; women are not left out, as the 'brothers and sisters' of 19:1 make clear.

a: My brothers are those who do the will of my Father
p: A short form of the saying in Matthew 12:50, Mark 3:35 and Luke 8:21.
b: The site's Matthew 12:50 reads: "For anyone who does what my Father in heaven wants, that person is my brother and my sister and my mother." The preacher's form names only 'brothers' and puts the sentence the other way round. Lake's margin gives all three Gospels (with OCR slips in the numbers). The saying ties the chapter's end to the next: 'let us do the will of the Father who called us' (10:1).

a: peace will run after us
p: We run after goodness (10:1), and peace runs after us: one Greek verb.
b: Greek diōxōmen, 'let us pursue' (10:1), and diōxetai, 'will pursue' (10:2). The preacher plays on Psalm 34:14, which 1 Peter 3:11 quotes: 'He must look for peace and run after it.' Here peace is the one doing the running.

a: people bring in human fears
t: A verse no one can mend
p: Lake says the Greek 'is very obscure' and may have lost a line.
b: Word for word the Greek says: 'For because of this reason it is not possible to find a person, who bring in human fears, having chosen rather the enjoyment here than the promise to come.' The singular 'a person' and the plural 'who' do not agree, and the object of 'find' is missing. Lake translates 'it is not possible for a man to find it', with a note: 'i.e. peace'. Lightfoot changed one word to read 'to prosper' (see the variant). Lake's footnote: 'even so the Greek is very obscure and probably there is a primitive corruption, perhaps the omission of a whole line.' The Plain English Translation follows Lake's sense and supplies 'peace'.
orig: οὐκ ἔστιν εὑρεῖν ἄνθρωπον, οἵτινες (ouk estin heurein anthrōpon, hoitines)

a: they keep on teaching evil to innocent souls
p: The only direct word about false teachers: they lead others astray and will be judged twice.
b: Greek kakodidaskalountes, 'teaching evil'. The preacher does not name them or their teaching. Lightfoot connected them with the denial of the resurrection of the flesh (9:1) and with an 'indifference' to fleshly lusts that followed from it, an early, unnamed form of the movements later called Gnostic, without the marks of Valentinus or Marcion. Their 'double judgment' is for their own sin and for leading others: compare James 3:1 ('we will receive a heavier judgment') and Matthew 18:6.

a: the prophetic word
p: The same unknown prophecy that 1 Clement 23:3-4 quotes, but with an ending of its own.
b: 1 Clement 23:3-4 quotes this passage as 'this Scripture', and the Plain English Translation uses the site's 1 Clement wording where the Greek agrees: "Miserable are the double-minded, those who waver in their soul and say, 'We heard these things back in our fathers' days, too.'" (1 Clement 23:3). The preacher's Greek has 'in their heart', 'long ago', and 'we have waited day after day and have seen none of them', where 1 Clement has 'we have grown old'. No book of the Bible has the passage. Lake's note at 11:4 says the extra clause 'seems to show that it is not derived from I Clement, but directly from the "prophetic word"', and his note on 1 Clement 23:3 mentions the suggestion that it comes from the lost book of Eldad and Modad. 2 Peter 3:4 answers the same complaint.

a: Miserable are the double-minded
p: Greek dipsychoi, 'two-souled', the word of James 1:8.
b: A dipsychos has 'two souls', one that trusts God's promise and one that doubts it. James uses the word: 'He is a double-minded man, never steady on any road he takes' (James 1:8). The preacher repeats it in 11:5 and 19:2, and makes the doubt concrete: people who have heard of Christ's coming since their fathers' time and have seen nothing happen.

a: Take a vine.
p: A vine passes through bare branches, shoots and sour grapes before the ripe cluster.
b: The prophecy answers the doubters with the farmer's year: the promise ripens slowly, but it ripens. The preacher's form is shorter than 1 Clement 23:4, which adds 'then a leaf, then a flower'. Jesus uses the fig tree in the same way: "When its branch is already soft and it pushes out its leaves, you know that summer is close" (Matthew 24:32).

a: In the same way my people have had turmoil and trouble
p: This clause is not in 1 Clement; Lake took it as a sign that both used the same lost book.
b: Lake's note: 'The additional clause at the end of this quotation seems to show that it is not derived from I Clement, but directly from the "prophetic word"'. 'My people' is God speaking, as in the prophets: the present 'turmoil and trouble' are the bare branches before the harvest of 'the good things'.

a: For the one who made the promise is trustworthy
p: The words of Hebrews 10:23, word for word in the Greek.
b: The Greek pistos gar ... ho epangeilamenos is that of Hebrews 10:23, so the Plain English Translation uses the site's wording: "for the one who made the promise is trustworthy" (Hebrews 10:23). Lake's margin puts the reference at 11:5. The second half, God paying each person for his works, is the teaching of Romans 2:6 ('He will pay back each person according to his works') and Revelation 22:12.

a: that no ear has heard and no eye has seen
p: Paul's 'as it is written' of 1 Corinthians 2:9, with ear before eye.
b: Paul quotes the saying with 'as it is written': "What no eye has seen and no ear has heard, and what has not come up into a human heart, all that God has prepared for those who love him" (1 Corinthians 2:9). Its source is debated; it is close to Isaiah 64:4. The preacher puts ear before eye and makes it describe 'the promises'. He uses the last words again in 14:5.

a: the day God will appear
p: Greek epiphaneia, the word for Christ's coming in the Pastoral Letters, here 'of God'.
b: Greek tēn hēmeran tēs epiphaneias tou theou, 'the day of the appearing of God'. In 1 Timothy 6:14 ('until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ') and Titus 2:13 the word names Christ's coming ('the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ'). The preacher speaks of 'God' appearing, and in 17:4 of 'his appearing', meaning the Lord's. 'We do not know the day' echoes Jesus: 'As for that day and hour, no one knows it' (Matthew 24:36).
orig: τῆς ἐπιφανείας τοῦ θεοῦ (tēs epiphaneias tou theou)

a: When the two are one
t: A saying from the Gospel of the Egyptians
p: Clement of Alexandria, answering Julius Cassianus, gives a fuller form of the saying and places it in the Gospel of the Egyptians.
b: Lake's note: 'The same saying, or very nearly so, is quoted from Cassianus by Clement of Alexandria (Strom. iii. 13), and the latter states that it is from the Gospel of the Egyptians.' In Clement's Greek, as Lightfoot prints it, Julius Cassianus gives the Lord's answer to Salome: Hotan to tēs aischynēs endyma patēsēte, kai hotan genētai ta dyo hen ..., 'When you trample on the garment of shame, and when the two become one, and the male with the female is neither male nor female.' Clement answers: 'In the four Gospels handed down to us we do not have the saying, but in the one according to the Egyptians.' The sermon's form has no 'garment of shame' and adds 'the outside like the inside'. Cassianus used the saying against marriage; in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, which gives the passage in Latin, Clement explains the male as anger and the female as desire. Lightfoot found 'nothing in these passages to suggest that Clement himself had read this gospel'. Lake adds that a similar saying in an Oxyrhynchus papyrus leaves the relation between these texts 'still unsolved'.
orig: Ὅταν ἔσται τὰ δύο ἕν (Hotan estai ta duo hen)

a: one soul lives in two bodies
p: The preacher's first explanation: the two are one when friends speak truth and share one soul.
b: This explanation is moral, not mystical. 'The two are one' when Christians speak the truth to one another and are of one soul without pretending. Luke says of the first church in Jerusalem that its believers 'had one heart and one soul' (Acts 4:32).

a: a brother who sees a sister should have no thought of her as female
p: The preacher reads the saying as a call to purity between Christian men and women.
b: The preacher does not say that Christians must give up marriage. He says that a Christian man looking at a Christian woman should not think of her as a woman, and she of him as a man: a rule of chaste behavior among 'brothers and sisters'. Lightfoot contrasted this with Clement of Alexandria, who refuted the use of the same saying against marriage and 'explains it in a mystical sense', and he saw in the sermon 'Encratite tendencies'. Paul's 'There is no male and female ... For all of you are one in Christ Jesus' (Galatians 3:28) speaks of standing before God, not of how men and women see one another, but the words are close. Lake's footnote on the last words gives a second reading (see the variant).

a: the people outside
p: Greek hoi exō, the New Testament's name for those who are not Christians.
b: Paul uses the same phrase: 'Be wise in the way you walk toward those outside' (Colossians 4:5; compare 1 Thessalonians 4:12 and 1 Corinthians 5:12). The preacher asks his hearers to please not only themselves but also outsiders, 'by our righteousness'. He is not telling them to be people-pleasers, which he forbids in the same sentence, but to live so that the name of God is not insulted.

a: My name is constantly insulted among all the Gentiles
p: Lake's margin gives Isaiah 52:5. The Greek Isaiah, which Paul also quotes, differs from the Hebrew.
b: The preacher's words follow the Greek Isaiah 52:5, which says the name is insulted 'among the Gentiles'. The site's Isaiah 52:5, made from the Hebrew, reads: 'and all day long, without stopping, / my name is treated with contempt', with no mention of the Gentiles. Paul quotes the Greek: "The name of God is insulted among the Gentiles because of you" (Romans 2:24). Like Paul, the preacher blames God's own people for the insult. 'Insulted' renders blasphēmeitai, as in the site's Romans 2:24.

a: Woe to the one because of whom my name is insulted
t: A second saying of unknown source
p: Lake: 'The source of this quotation is unknown.'
b: No book of the Bible has these words. Lake's footnote says only that 'the source of this quotation is unknown'. The thought is that of Isaiah 52:5 and Romans 2:24, joined to a 'woe' like Jesus' "woe to the person through whom the snare comes!" (Matthew 18:7).

a: When you do not do what I want
p: The answer is in the Lord's voice: 'what I want'.
b: After his own question, 'How is it insulted?', the preacher answers in the first person, as if the Lord were still speaking. Lake prints the answer as the start of 13:3. The shift shows how freely the preacher moves between quoting and explaining.

a: God's sayings
p: Greek ta logia tou theou: here the words of Jesus the church teaches.
b: The phrase is the one Paul uses of the Scriptures given to Israel: 'they were put in charge of the oracles of God' (Romans 3:2). The preacher uses it for the teaching outsiders hear 'from our mouths', and gives an example in 13:4, a saying of Jesus. Lightfoot took this, with 'God says' in 13:4, as a sign of how high the sermon places the words of Jesus.
orig: τὰ λόγια τοῦ θεοῦ (ta logia tou theou)

a: some myth and delusion
p: Pagans heard Christian teaching with admiration, and then dismissed it when they saw Christians' lives.
b: Greek mython tina kai planēn, 'a myth and a deception'. The preacher gives an outsider's view of the church: the words are 'beautiful and great', but the lives do not match, so the whole thing must be a fable. The same concern runs through 1 Peter: "Keep your way of life fine and good among the Gentiles" (1 Peter 2:12).

a: that God says
p: A saying of Jesus close to Luke 6:32 and 6:35 is introduced with 'God says'.
b: The saying is close to Luke 6:32 and 6:35 ("If you love the people who love you, what thanks do you have coming for that?"; "keep loving your enemies"). The Greek charis is 'thanks' in the site's Luke and 'credit' here, because the preacher uses it twice in a balanced pair. Lightfoot pointed out that the preacher 'introduces a saying of our Lord in the Gospels with the words "God saith"', and used the fact in dating the sermon. It agrees with his opening words: we must think of Jesus Christ as of God (1:1).

a: the first church, the spiritual one
p: The church existed in God's plan, or in heaven, before the sun and moon were made.
b: Lightfoot called this 'doctrine of an eternal Church' a development of Paul's teaching that God chose a people in Christ 'before the world was founded' (Ephesians 1:4), and placed the preacher 'midway in point of development ... between this teaching of S. Paul and the doctrine of the Valentinians', a Gnostic school that spoke of a heavenly being called 'Church'. He took this as a sign that the sermon was written before Valentinus taught. In the Bible, compare 'the Jerusalem above' that 'is our mother' (Galatians 4:26).

a: before the sun and moon
p: Lightfoot traced the phrase to the Greek of Psalm 72, read of Christ.
b: Lightfoot thought the words were 'probably taken from' Psalm 72:5 and 72:17 in Greek, where the king's name lasts 'before the sun' and 'before the moon'. He noted that the Hebrew means 'as long as' the sun and moon last (the site's Psalm 72:5: 'as long as the sun lasts, / and while the moon stands'), and that Justin Martyr (Dialogue 64, as Lightfoot cites him) read the Greek of Christ, 'that he was before the sun'. The preacher applies it to the church.

a: My house has become a cave for bandits
p: Jeremiah 7:11, the verse Jesus used in the Temple.
b: Jeremiah asked: 'Has this house, the one called by my name, become a cave for bandits in your eyes?' (Jeremiah 7:11). Jesus joined it with Isaiah 56:7 when he drove out the traders: "you are turning it into a cave for bandits" (Matthew 21:13). The preacher's form is a statement, 'my house has become', and he applies it to those in the church who do not do the Lord's will: they belong to the 'cave', not to the 'church of life'.

a: the living church is the body of Christ
p: Lake prints 'Church is the body of Christ' as a quotation of Ephesians 1:23.
b: Paul writes: 'The church is his body, the fullness of the one who is filling all things in every way' (Ephesians 1:23; compare Colossians 1:24). The preacher adds 'living' and takes for granted that his hearers know the teaching ('I do not think you are unaware').

a: God made the human being male and female
t: Male and female: Christ and the church
p: Genesis 1:27 read as a picture of Christ and the church.
b: The site's Genesis 1:27 ends: 'male and female he created them'. The preacher's Greek follows the Greek Genesis, 'God made the human being male and female', and reads the male as Christ and the female as the church. Paul made a similar move with Genesis 2:24: 'This mystery is a great one. And I am speaking about Christ and about the church' (Ephesians 5:32).

a: the Books
p: The Old Testament and the apostles' writings named side by side as authorities.
b: Greek ta biblia kai hoi apostoloi. Lightfoot: the preacher 'distinguishes between the Old and New Testament: the former he styles "the Books," "the Bible" (τὰ βιβλία), while the latter (or a part of it) is designated "the Apostles".' The word biblia is the source of the English 'Bible'. Lightfoot used this way of naming them to place the sermon before the last quarter of the second century, when writers spoke of the four Gospels and the apostles' letters more fully. The Greek manuscript C lacks the verb 'say', and the Syriac adds 'of the prophets' after 'the books' (see the variant).

a: but he was revealed in the last days to save us
p: The Greek verb has no subject; grammar favors the church, Lake's translation says Jesus.
b: Greek ephanerōthē de ep' eschatōn tōn hēmerōn, hina hēmas sōsē, 'and was revealed at the last of the days, that ... might save us'. Lake's note: 'The translation "she was made … that she might save us" is grammatically more probable, but seems to be excluded both by the context and by the history of doctrine.' The Plain English Translation follows Lake. The words echo 1 Peter 1:20, of Christ: 'he has been brought into the open in the last of the times, for your sake'. Verse 14:3 then says the church too was revealed, 'in the flesh of Christ'.

a: the copy of the spirit
p: The flesh is a copy; the spirit is the original. Corrupt the copy, lose the original.
b: Greek antitypos, 'copy, counterpart', and to authentikon, 'the original', the word for an original document as against its copies. Hebrews uses antitypa of the earthly sanctuary, 'a copy of the true one' (Hebrews 9:24). The preacher's argument is that what we do to the flesh, the visible church in its members' bodies, we do to the spirit it copies. Lake writes 'Spirit' with a capital; the Plain English Translation keeps 'spirit' lowercase here and in 14:4, where the spirit is said to be Christ, and capitalizes only 'Holy Spirit'.

a: the spirit is Christ
p: The preacher identifies the spirit with Christ, as Paul says 'the Lord is the Spirit'.
b: The thought matches 9:5, where Christ 'was spirit at first'. Paul says 'Now, the Lord is the Spirit' (2 Corinthians 3:17). Lightfoot's paraphrase reads 'the Spirit, that is ... Christ'. The words allow two readings: 'spirit' may name Christ's divine nature, or the Son and the Holy Spirit may not be kept apart. The preacher's practical point is plain: whoever abuses the flesh abuses the church, and will not share in Christ.

a: what the Lord has prepared
p: The end of 1 Corinthians 2:9 again (see 11:7).
b: The preacher closes his teaching on the flesh with the last words of the saying he used at 11:7: 'all that God has prepared for those who love him' (1 Corinthians 2:9). Here it is 'the Lord' who prepares, and for 'his chosen'. What the flesh can receive, 'life and incorruption', cannot be put into words.

a: the advice I have given about self-control
p: The preacher himself names his subject: self-control.
b: Greek symboulia peri enkrateias, 'advice about self-control'. The words look back over the whole sermon, and especially over chapters 8-14 on keeping the flesh pure. They also show the preacher's view of what he is doing: giving counsel, not issuing commands. 'Will not regret it' (ou metanoēsei) uses the verb for 'repent', which runs through the sermon: whoever takes the advice will not need to repent of taking it.

a: save both himself and me
t: Saving the hearer and the preacher
p: The preacher's salvation is tied to his hearers', as in 1 Timothy 4:16 and James 5:20.
b: Paul tells Timothy: 'If you do this, you will save yourself and the people who listen to you as well' (1 Timothy 4:16). James ends his letter: 'whoever turns a sinner back from the wrong road he wandered onto will save his soul from death' (James 5:20). The preacher says it again at 19:1: 'so that you may save both yourselves and the one who reads among you'.

a: While you are still speaking, I will say, 'Look, I am here.'
p: Isaiah 58:9, with the 'while you are still speaking' of Isaiah 65:24.
b: The site's Isaiah 58:9 reads: 'You will shout for help, and he will say, "I am here."' Isaiah 65:24 has: 'while they are still talking, I will have heard'. The preacher's saying joins the two thoughts, God answering before the prayer is finished. He draws the lesson in 15:4: God is more ready to give than we are to ask.

a: burning like an oven
t: The day burning like an oven
p: Malachi 4:1 (Lake's margin), with Isaiah 34:4 behind 'the heavens will melt'.
b: The site's Malachi 4:1 reads: "For look, the day is coming, burning like an oven." The preacher calls it 'the day of judgment'. Isaiah 34:4 in Greek speaks of the 'powers of the heavens' melting; the Hebrew (the site's Isaiah 34:4) says 'The whole army of heaven will rot'. 2 Peter 3:10-12 speaks of the heavens dissolving and the elements melting on 'God's day'.

a: like lead melting in the fire
p: Why only 'some' of the heavens? Lake gives two answers.
b: Lake's note on 'some': 'Possibly the text is corrupt: Lightfoot's conjecture would be translated, "the powers of heaven," but the text may be defended as a reference to the early Christian belief in seven concentric heavens surrounding the Earth.' If there are several heavens, the lower ones may melt while God's own heaven stands. Paul tells of a man 'snatched up as far as the third heaven' (2 Corinthians 12:2). The picture of lead is a metalworker's: the earth runs like molten metal in the fire of judgment.

a: the secret and open deeds of people will be brought to light
p: Judgment brings everything into the open.
b: Compare "on the day when God judges what people keep secret" (Romans 2:16) and 1 Corinthians 4:5. The preacher speaks of 'deeds', in keeping with his teaching that we confess Christ by what we do (4:3).

a: So almsgiving is good, as repentance for sin is
p: The preacher teaches that giving to the poor 'lightens' sin. The churches read such teaching differently.
b: Greek eleēmosynē, 'almsgiving, gifts to the poor'. The verse belongs to a Jewish tradition found in Daniel 4:27 ('Break with your sins by doing what is right, and with your wrongs by showing mercy to the poor') and above all Tobit: 'Alms rescue from death, and they cleanse away every sin' (Tobit 12:9). The preacher's first words are compressed: almsgiving is good, 'as repentance for sin'. Lake translates 'even as penitence for sin'. Whether giving can make amends for sin, or is only the fruit of a forgiven life, is a question the churches answer differently: see the cards at Proverbs 16:6 and Tobit 4, which the site already gives. Tobit is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox churches and not for Protestants; 2 Clement is Scripture for none.

a: Fasting is better than prayer
p: No book of the Bible ranks the three this way.
b: Jesus treats giving, prayer and fasting together, as the three works of piety to be done in secret (Matthew 6:1-18), and Tobit 12:8 praises prayer and alms together. The preacher's ranking, fasting above prayer and almsgiving above both, goes beyond anything in the 66 books, which never set prayer below fasting. In Claude's analysis this is a place where the sermon goes beyond the Bible and sits uneasily with it, since the Bible's prayers and fasts are always joined (Ezra 8:23; Acts 13:3).

a: love lays a cover over a great number of sins
p: The words of 1 Peter 4:8, word for word in the Greek.
b: The preacher's Greek is that of 1 Peter 4:8, so the Plain English Translation uses the site's wording: "love lays a cover over a great number of sins" (1 Peter 4:8). Behind both stands Proverbs 10:12 ('love lays a cover over all wrongdoing'), and James 5:20 says the same of turning a sinner back. Lake's margin gives 1 Peter 4:8.

a: prayer from a good conscience rescues from death
p: Tobit says alms rescue from death; the preacher gives the line to prayer.
b: Tobit 12:9 reads: "Alms rescue from death, and they cleanse away every sin." The preacher has 'prayer from a good conscience rescues from death', and keeps for almsgiving the last word, that it 'lightens the weight of sin' (Greek kouphisma, 'a lightening'). The picture is of sin as a load.

a: pull people away from idols and teach them
p: The church had commandments to draw pagans away from idols and teach them.
b: Greek apo tōn eidōlōn apospan kai katēchein, 'to draw away from the idols and to instruct'. The verb katēcheō, 'instruct by word of mouth', is the source of 'catechism' and 'catechumen'. The preacher argues from the greater effort to the lesser: if we must win and teach pagans, how much more must we not let a believer be lost. Compare Matthew 28:19-20 and James 5:19-20.

a: while the elders are warning us
p: Office or age? The context points to church leaders who teach.
b: Greek hypo tōn presbyterōn, 'by the elders'. The word can mean older people or the church's leaders. Here the elders warn the congregation in its meeting, and in 17:5 the lost confess that they did not obey 'the elders who told us about our salvation', so the Plain English Translation reads the office, 'elders', as the site does elsewhere. The preacher speaks as one of the hearers ('warning us'). Lightfoot thought this 'a very common rhetorical figure, by which the speaker places himself on a level with his audience', and held that the preacher was himself a church leader. Harnack, as Lightfoot reports him, inferred that the preacher was a layman.

a: think the same way
p: Paul's phrase in Philippians 2:2.
b: Greek to auto phronountes, as Paul writes: 'think the same way' (Philippians 2:2; compare Romans 15:5). Lake's printed margin points to Romans 12:16 and Philippians 2:2. The preacher joins it to the picture of being 'gathered together for life', which prepares for the Lord's word about gathering the nations (17:4).

a: I am coming to gather all the nations, tribes and languages
p: Isaiah 66:18 in Greek, with 'tribes' added; the preacher calls it the Lord's word.
b: The site's Isaiah 66:18, made from the Hebrew, reads: 'The time is coming to gather all nations and languages, and they will come and see my glory.' The Greek Isaiah begins 'I am coming', which the preacher reads as the coming of Christ, 'the day of his appearing'. He adds 'tribes', a word that recalls Revelation's 'every nation and tribe and people and language' (Revelation 7:9). In 17:5 he continues with Isaiah 66:18's 'see my glory' and ends with 66:24 (see 7:6).

a: redeem us, each one according to his works
p: An odd pairing to modern ears: 'redeem' and 'according to works'.
b: Greek lytrōsetai, 'he will redeem, set free by payment'. The preacher joins it to the Bible's teaching that each will be repaid 'according to his works' (Romans 2:6; Revelation 22:12). He does not say that works earn the redemption; his concern throughout is that a faith which does not show in deeds is not confession at all (4:1-3). How faith and works relate in salvation is set out on the topic page on justification and in the cards at Romans 3-4 and James 2.

a: the kingship of the world in Jesus' hands
p: Revelation 11:15: 'The kingdom of the world has become our Lord's and his Messiah's.'
b: Greek to basileion tou kosmou en tō Iēsou, 'the kingship of the world in Jesus'. Lake translates 'the sovereignty of the world given to Jesus'. Basileion is the word rendered 'palace' in 6:9 ('God's palace'); there the hearers enter it, here the world's rule is seen in Jesus' hands, so the Plain English Translation gives each place its sense. Revelation 11:15 announces: 'The kingdom of the world / has become our Lord's and his Messiah's'. The astonishment of the unbelievers recalls the Wisdom of Solomon, where the wicked see the righteous man they mocked counted 'among the sons of God' and say 'we fools!' (Wisdom of Solomon 5:4-5).

a: we did not obey the elders who told us about our salvation
p: The elders are the ones who announced salvation to the congregation.
b: In the confession of the lost, the elders' task is to 'tell us about our salvation', that is, to preach. With 17:3 this is the sermon's only picture of the church's leaders. It names no overseer (bishop). Whether that silence means anything for the sermon's date or place, the sermon alone cannot show.

a: There will be hope for the one who has served God with his whole heart
p: The righteous see the punishment of the lost and give glory to God.
b: The scene comes from Isaiah 66:24, where the people 'go out and look at the corpses' of the rebels. The preacher gives the righteous words of praise, not of gloating: they see that hope belonged to those who served God wholeheartedly. The sermon describes the scene only to move its hearers to repent now (18:1).

a: those who give thanks
p: Greek eucharistountōn, 'those giving thanks'.
b: The verb is eucharisteō, 'give thanks', the word from which 'Eucharist' later came. Here it describes the grateful who have served God, set against 'the godless who are judged'. The sermon does not mention the church's meal.

a: a sinner through and through
p: Greek panthamartōlos, 'completely sinful': the preacher counts himself among those who must repent.
b: The preacher interrupts his appeal to speak of himself: 'all-sinful', not yet free of temptation, 'surrounded by the devil's tools', yet trying to come near righteousness. It recalls Paul's 'among them I am the first' (1 Timothy 1:15). It also explains his tone: he says 'let us' throughout because he includes himself.

a: brothers and sisters
p: Here, for the first time, the preacher names the women in his congregation.
b: Greek adelphoi kai adelphai, 'brothers and sisters', again in 20:2. Lightfoot called this the proof, once the ending was found, that 'the work is plainly not a letter, but a homily, a sermon': the speaker addresses his hearers 'more than once towards the close as "brothers and sisters"'. Until 19:1 the Plain English Translation has said 'brothers', so that the change shows (see 1:1).

a: after the God of truth
p: The sermon was read after the reading of Scripture, which the preacher calls 'the God of truth'.
b: Lightfoot read the words as meaning that the sermon came 'after the "God of truth" has been first heard in the scriptures', and compared Justin Martyr's description of Sunday worship in Rome, where 'the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time permits', and then the leader gives teaching (Justin, First Apology 67). Lightfoot reports that Zahn and Donaldson proposed to change 'God' to 'word', but he kept the text, since the preacher elsewhere introduces a saying of Jesus with 'God says' (13:4). Which Scripture was read, Old Testament or New, the sermon does not say. 'What is written' then means that reading.
orig: μετὰ τὸν θεὸν τῆς ἀληθείας (meta ton theon tēs alētheias)

a: I am reading you an appeal
p: The preacher reads from a written text: he is not speaking off the cuff.
b: Greek anaginōskō hymin enteuxin, 'I read to you an appeal'. Lake translates 'exhortation'. This verse is why Lake calls the work 'a letter only in form, and scarcely in that': the writer 'distinctly states ... that he is reading aloud, and implies that he is doing so in a meeting for religious worship'. Lightfoot thought the sermon 'was not an extempore address, but was delivered from a manuscript', which would explain why it was kept and copied, though he allowed that it might have been taken down by shorthand writers and the references to reading added later.

a: the one who reads among you
p: Lake: 'probable though not quite certain' that this means an order of Readers in the church.
b: Greek ton anaginōskonta en hymin, 'the one reading among you', the preacher himself. Lake's note: 'It is probable though not quite certain that this refer to a definite order of "Readers" in the Church.' Later churches had readers (lectors) as a recognized ministry; the sermon shows only that someone read the sermon, and perhaps the Scripture before it, aloud. Revelation 1:3 blesses "the one who reads the words of this prophecy out loud" (Revelation 1:3) and those who hear.

a: our understanding has gone dark from empty desires
p: Ephesians 4:18 (Lake's margin).
b: Paul says of the Gentiles: 'Their understanding has gone dark' (Ephesians 4:18). The preacher's Greek has the same verb and noun, and he applies the words to the church: even believers can do wrong without knowing it, because double-mindedness and unbelief cloud the mind. That is why, he says, no one should resent being warned.

a: the immortal fruit of the resurrection
p: Greek trygēsousin, 'they will harvest', used of picking grapes.
b: The vine of 11:3 returns: those who wait through the bare months will gather the ripe fruit. Here the harvest is the resurrection, the sermon's great hope (9:1-5). Paul calls the risen Christ "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20).

a: He will live again above with the fathers
p: Greek anabiōsas, 'having come back to life'. Resurrection, or life with God after death?
b: The preacher says the godly will 'live again above with the fathers', that is, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the righteous of Israel (compare Matthew 8:11). 'Live again' points to the resurrection of 19:3; 'above' points to heaven. The sermon does not say whether this happens at death or at the last day. On the site, the cards at 2 Corinthians 5 and Philippians 1 give the churches' views on what happens between death and the resurrection.

a: God's slaves
p: Greek douloi, 'slaves': the New Testament's word for believers in relation to God.
b: The site renders doulos 'slave', as in Jude 1:1 ('From Jude, a slave of Jesus Christ'), because Greek had a separate word for a hired servant. In the Roman world a slave belonged wholly to a master; the early Christians took the word for themselves as a mark of total belonging to God. The preacher sets 'God's slaves' in hard straits against the wicked growing rich, the old complaint of Psalm 73:3 ('I was jealous of the boasters / as I watched the wicked thrive') and Jeremiah 12:1.
orig: τοὺς τοῦ θεοῦ δούλους (tous tou theou doulous)

a: We are competing in the trial of the living God
t: The trial of the living God
p: The games return: life now is the training; the crown is in the life to come.
b: Greek theou zōntos peiran athloumen kai gymnazometha, 'we compete in a test of the living God and are trained'. The words come from the athlete's world (athleō, 'compete'; gymnazō, 'train', the root of 'gymnasium'), and take up chapter 7 again. Lake translates 'we are contending in the contest of the living God'. 'Trial' renders peira, 'test, attempt'.

a: reverence for God
p: Greek theosebeia, 'reverence for God', set against business.
b: If God paid at once, people would serve him for profit, 'training ourselves in business and not in reverence for God'. The point is that of the Accuser's question, "Is it for no reason that Job fears God?" (Job 1:9), and of 1 Timothy 6:5, which warns against those who "suppose godliness is a source of profit" (1 Timothy 6:5).

a: God's judgment strikes a spirit that is not righteous and loads it with chains
p: Lake reads a general truth; Harnack saw the fall of Satan.
b: The Greek verbs are aorists, 'struck' and 'weighed down'. Lake's note: 'This translation takes the aorist as gnomic, and regards "spirit" as meaning a human spirit. But Harnack prefers to take the aorist as historical and refers the passage to the fall of Satan.' A 'gnomic' aorist states a general truth, as English does with the present ('God's judgment strikes'). The Plain English Translation follows Lake. Harnack's reading would point to angels 'kept in everlasting chains' (Jude 1:6; 2 Peter 2:4).

a: To the only God, who cannot be seen
p: The doxology borrows from 1 Timothy 1:17 and calls Christ 'Founder of incorruption'.
b: The site's 1 Timothy 1:17 reads: 'To the King of the ages, who cannot decay and cannot be seen, the only God: honor and glory to him forever and ever. Amen.' Lake's margin gives the verse. 'Founder' renders archēgos, the title of Christ in Hebrews 2:10 ('the Founder of their salvation') and 12:2. 'The truth and the life of heaven' recalls 2 Timothy 1:10, where Christ has brought 'life and immortality out into the light'.

a: The second letter of Clement to the Corinthians.
p: The subscription Lake prints names Clement, but the sermon never names its author.
b: Lake prints at the end Klēmentos pros Korinthious epistolē b, 'Of Clement to the Corinthians, letter 2'. The sermon itself names no author, no city and no event. Eusebius wrote that 'there is said to be a second epistle of Clement. But we do not know that this is recognized like the former, for we do not find that the ancients have made any use of it' (Church History 3.38.4), and Jerome that 'there is also a second Epistle under his name which is rejected by earlier writers' (Lives of Illustrious Men 15). Lake: 'it cannot have been written by the author of I. Clement'. Lightfoot explained the name: the sermon was kept at Corinth with 1 Clement and copied after it, and in copying the two came to seem 'of the same kind and by the same author'. The site therefore calls it 2 Clement, by custom, and treats it as an anonymous sermon.
orig: Κλήμεντος πρὸς Κορινθίους ἐπιστολὴ β (Klēmentos pros Korinthious epistolē b)
